title: Reverse a String (Which You Cannot Mutate)
statement:
`String` in Java is immutable: once created, its characters never
change, and there is no method on it that rewrites them in place -- not
for one character, not for all of them. That is not a missing convenience;
it is a guarantee the whole language leans on (string literals are safely
shared, `String` is safe as a `HashMap` key). Reversing a string in Java
always means producing a *new* string, never mutating the one you were
given.

## Your function

```
public static String reversed(String text);
```

Return a new string containing `text`'s characters in reverse order.
`text` may be empty. `text` itself must be left exactly as it was --
which, for an immutable type, is automatic once you stop trying to
change it and start building something new instead.

## Watch out

- **There is no `ReverseInPlace` in Java the way there might be in a
  language with mutable strings or reference parameters.** Reassigning
  the parameter itself (`text = something;`) only rebinds the local
  variable inside this function -- it has no effect the caller can ever
  see, because Java passes the string *reference* by value: the caller's
  own reference still points at the original, unreversed string object.
- **`text.toCharArray()` gives you a mutable `char[]` copy of the
  characters** -- swap elements of *that* array freely, then build the
  result with `new String(reversedChars)`. The array is yours; `text`
  itself is never touched.
- An empty string and a one-character string both need zero swaps -- a
  two-pointer loop that stops once the indices meet or cross handles
  both without a separate check for either.

tests.name: an empty string reverses to itself
a palindrome reverses to itself
tests.description: Checks the characters were actually rebuilt in reverse, not just returned unchanged -- a function that returns text as-is passes this by accident.

tests.name: spaces and punctuation are ordinary characters
